newsitem.title: UK: Britain's building societies in dark on regulatory status.
newsitem.headline: Britain's building societies in dark on regulatory status.

text.p: Britain's building societies must continue to be regulated differently from other financial institutions, leading figures in the mutually-owned sector said at their annual conference on Wednesday.

Most delegates said they were surprised that building societies had not been mentioned in the Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's proposals to reshape Britain's financial regulatory framework on Tuesday.

"Building societies and mortgages were not mentioned so we don't know where we are going to be," Adrian Cole, director general of the Building Societies Association (BSA), told Reuters in an interview.

Coles, along with other building society officials, said one factor distinguishing the mutual societies, which are owned by their borrowers and savers, from banks and other financial service providers was that they had not been tainted by the sort of scandals which had hit others.

"Uniquely the Building Societies Commission (BSC) has not had a major crisis in the last 10 years," Coles said. The BSC was set up under the Building Societies Act of 1996 as the regulator and supervisor of the sector.
Geoffrey Fitchew, chairman of the BSC, told Reuters that the role of the BSC would be "discussed and debated as the shape of the SIB (Securities and Investment Board) becomes clear".

Fitchew said the question would hinge on whether there was room for a specialised niche regulator for a specialised sector, such as the building society sector, while still achieving the economies of scale demanded by the new regulatory approach.

Earlier Fitchew told the conference that no decision had yet been taken on changes to the existing regulatory arrangements for building societies, but he stressed that the views of the BSA and the building societies themselves would be heard.

"We act under statute at the moment. We are happy to go on doing the job as long as the government want us to do it," he told Reuters, adding that an "effective and sensible legislative structure" already existed in the 1997 Building Societies Act.
Supporters of the BSC were quick to point out its strengths and call for its specialist knowledge not to be lost.

"The regulator has done a very good job in a very difficult period," Coles said, pointing out that the building societies had come through a major housing recession and cuts in state benefits which could have threatened their livelihoood.

Kenneth Culley, chief executive of the Portman Building Society, told Reuters that if the system had to be changed then he would like to see the BSC lifted as a whole and placed within the new "super regulator" proposed by the government.
Culley was also at pains to stress that the 16 million smaller savers with building societies had not been exposed to any losses over the years.
"Never in living memory has anyone lost a penny as a result of having money with a building society," he said.

While building societies -- the traditional lenders to Britain's home-owners -- remain in the dark as to the shape of their regulatory landscape under the government plans, a number of delegates admitted it would be strange if they were left outside the new body.

The enlarged SIB, which will take on the banking supervisory role of the Bank of England as well as the roles of the three so-called "frontline" self-regulators, is intended to enhance investor protection, be more effective and save money.

But while building societies are making a point of stressing their difference to banks and other publicly quoted financial services providers, it could arouse suspicion among the general public if they were treated differently.

Because they do not have shareholders, the societies are making much of providing better savings and borrowing rates to their customer-members. The BSA's Coles said building societies are different and the society would be making this and other points to the Treasury.
